text: Why does solid copper conduct electricity?
options: Copper atoms move throughout the lattice
Delocalized electrons move through the metal
Copper ions leave the lattice as a current
scheme: Metallic bonding contains mobile delocalized electrons that transport charge through the solid.

text: Which comparison best explains the higher melting temperature of magnesium than sodium using a simple metallic-bonding model?
options: Mg has more shells than Na
Mg contributes more delocalized electrons and has a greater cation charge
scheme: Mg contributes two delocalized electrons per atom and forms more highly charged, relatively small metal cations, strengthening attraction to the electron sea.

text: Which structural change occurs when ethene forms poly(ethene)?
options: The C=C double bond opens and new C–C links join monomers
Carbon atoms are removed as carbon dioxide
Water is released from every monomer
The monomer becomes an ionic lattice
scheme: Addition polymerization uses the carbon–carbon double bond to connect monomer units; no small by-product is required.

text: A diol reacts with a dicarboxylic acid to make a condensation polymer. Which linkage is formed?
scheme: An alcohol group and carboxyl group react to make an ester linkage with elimination of a small molecule such as water.

text: Which statement explains the decrease in atomic radius across period 3?
options: An extra principal shell is added at every element
Nuclear charge increases while shielding by inner shells changes little
Electrons are removed from every atom
Protons are lost across the period
scheme: Electrons are added to the same principal shell while increasing proton number strengthens attraction; the outer electron cloud contracts.

text: A transition-metal complex appears blue in white light. What can be deduced?
options: It emits only blue light through radioactive decay
It absorbs the complementary region of visible light
Its d orbitals must all be completely filled
Its colour is unrelated to electronic transitions
scheme: Visible light absorbed can promote an electron between split d-orbital energies. Transmitted/reflected light has a complementary observed colour.

text: Which compound is a ketone?
scheme: CH₃COCH₃ contains a carbonyl bonded to carbon groups on both sides; this is a ketone functional group.

text: An organic compound shows two proton NMR signals with integration ratio 3:2. Which structure is consistent?
scheme: CH₃CH₂Br has a three-H methyl environment and a two-H methylene environment. The other options have either one or three proton environments.

text: In an exothermic reaction carried out in an insulated cup, what is usually observed?
options: Products have greater enthalpy than reactants
scheme: An exothermic system transfers heat to its surroundings; the solution commonly warms and the reaction has negative ΔH.

text: A solution of mass 100.0 g warms by 5.0 K. Using c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, what heat has the solution absorbed?
Bond enthalpies are H–H = 436, Cl–Cl = 243 and H–Cl = 431 kJ mol⁻¹. Estimate ΔH for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g).
scheme: ΔH ≈ bonds broken − bonds formed = (436 + 243) − 2(431) = −183 kJ mol⁻¹.

text: Which species has a standard enthalpy of formation of zero by definition at 298 K?
scheme: The standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state is zero; oxygen’s standard state at 298 K is O₂(g).

text: Which product is associated with incomplete combustion of a hydrocarbon and is toxic?
scheme: An insufficient oxygen supply can produce carbon monoxide, which is toxic; complete combustion would instead produce carbon dioxide and water.

text: Which statement describes a hydrogen fuel cell during operation?
options: It converts chemical energy directly into electrical energy
It stores all energy only as an increase in temperature
It always requires electrical energy to force its overall discharge reaction
Its fuel is regenerated indefinitely without input
scheme: A fuel cell combines a continuously supplied fuel and oxidant in electrochemical reactions that convert chemical energy directly to electrical energy.

text: For a reaction with ΔH° = +40 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS° = +100 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, at what temperatures is ΔG° negative, assuming both quantities are temperature independent?
scheme: Convert ΔS° to 0.100 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. ΔG° = 40 − 0.100T is negative for T > 400 K.

text: If K > 1 at a specified temperature, what is the sign of ΔG° for the reaction as written?
scheme: ΔG° = −RT ln K. When K > 1, ln K is positive and ΔG° is negative.

text: For 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g), 3.0 mol H₂ and 1.0 mol O₂ are mixed. What is the maximum amount of H₂O?
scheme: O₂ is limiting: 1.0 mol O₂ consumes 2.0 mol H₂ and makes 2.0 mol H₂O; 1.0 mol H₂ remains.

text: An experiment produces 7.2 g of product from a theoretical yield of 9.0 g. What is the percentage yield?
scheme: Percentage yield = actual/theoretical × 100 = 7.2/9.0 × 100 = 80%.

text: How does a catalyst increase reaction rate?
options: It raises the temperature of every reaction
It provides a pathway with lower activation energy
It increases the enthalpy difference between products and reactants
It shifts every equilibrium to the products
scheme: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy so a greater fraction of collisions can lead to reaction; ΔH and equilibrium position are unchanged.

text: For rate = k[A]²[B], what happens to the rate when [A] doubles and [B] halves at constant temperature?
scheme: The factor is 2² × 1/2 = 2. The rate doubles, while k remains constant at unchanged temperature.

text: What is true at dynamic chemical equilibrium in a closed system?
options: Reactants and products always have equal concentrations
Both forward and reverse reactions stop
The forward and reverse reaction rates are equal
scheme: At dynamic equilibrium both reactions continue at equal rates; concentrations are constant but not necessarily equal.

text: For a reaction at fixed temperature, Q = 0.20 and K = 4.0. Which direction is favoured as equilibrium is approached?
options: No net change because Q is non-zero
Neither; Q cannot be compared with K
scheme: Q < K, so net forward reaction increases the product-to-reactant ratio until Q reaches K.

text: What is the pH of a solution with [H⁺] = 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³?
scheme: pH = −log₁₀(2.0 × 10⁻³) = 2.70 to two decimal places.

text: A buffer contains a weak acid HA and its conjugate base A⁻ at equal concentrations. What is the relationship between pH and pKₐ?
scheme: Kₐ = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]. When [A⁻] = [HA], [H⁺] = Kₐ, so pH = pKₐ.

text: In a voltaic cell, where does oxidation occur?
options: At both electrodes simultaneously by definition
scheme: Oxidation occurs at the anode. In a voltaic cell the anode supplies electrons and is the negative electrode.

text: Standard reduction potentials are E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V and E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V. What is E°cell for the spontaneous zinc–copper cell?
scheme: Cu²⁺ is reduced at the cathode and Zn is oxidized at the anode. E°cell = 0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V.

text: Which process produces chlorine radicals from Cl₂ under UV light?
options: Heterolytic fission with both electrons on one atom
Homolytic fission with one electron on each atom
scheme: Homolytic fission gives one bonding electron to each chlorine atom: Cl₂ → 2Cl•.

text: Which equation is a termination step in methane chlorination?
scheme: Termination combines two radicals to form a non-radical product without regenerating another radical.

text: Which statement defines a nucleophile?
options: It donates a pair of electrons to form a bond
It must always have a positive charge
It accepts a proton in every possible reaction
It contains no lone pairs or π electrons
scheme: A nucleophile donates both electrons of a newly formed bond. It can be neutral or negatively charged.

text: Which rate equation is consistent with a one-step SN2 reaction between a primary halogenoalkane RBr and OH⁻?
scheme: Both the halogenoalkane and nucleophile participate in the concerted bimolecular substitution step; the rate is first order in each.

text: Explain why a pure metal can be both malleable and electrically conducting.
scheme: Metal cations are surrounded by delocalized electrons in a metallic lattice [1].
The electrons are mobile and carry electrical charge [1].
Layers can change position while non-directional attraction between cations and electrons is maintained, allowing deformation [1].

text: Draw or describe the repeating unit of the addition polymer formed from CH₂=CHCl. Explain why its formation can have 100% atom economy.
scheme: Open the C=C double bond to give the backbone repeating unit –CH₂–CHCl– [1].
Show the repeating unit in brackets with bonds continuing through the brackets and subscript n [1].
All monomer atoms are incorporated in the polymer; no small-molecule by-product is required [1].

text: A polyester is made from HO–CH₂–CH₂–OH and HOOC–CH₂–COOH. Describe its repeat linkage and explain the small molecule released.
scheme: The alcohol groups of the diol react with carboxyl groups of the dicarboxylic acid [1].
An ester linkage –C(=O)–O– forms between monomer residues [1].
A valid repeat unit is –O–CH₂–CH₂–O–C(=O)–CH₂–C(=O)– with continuous backbone bonds [1].
Water is eliminated when an –OH and H combine during formation of each ester linkage [1].

text: Predict and explain the reaction when chlorine is added to aqueous potassium bromide. Include an ionic equation.
scheme: Chlorine oxidizes bromide ions to bromine because chlorine is the stronger oxidizing halogen [1].
Cl₂(aq) + 2Br⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + Br₂(aq) [1].
An orange/brown colour from bromine develops; Br⁻ loses electrons while chlorine gains electrons [1].

text: Give the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ and explain why it is classified as a secondary alcohol.
scheme: The longest chain contains four carbons: butane parent [1].
The hydroxyl group receives the lowest possible locant, giving butan-2-ol [1].
The carbon bearing –OH is bonded to two other carbon atoms, so the alcohol is secondary [1].

text: A compound has molecular formula C₂H₄O₂. Its IR spectrum has a broad absorption spanning approximately 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ and a strong carbonyl absorption. Its ¹H NMR contains a 3H singlet and a 1H downfield signal. Deduce a structure and justify it.
scheme: The formula and carbonyl absorption support a carbonyl-containing molecule [1].
The very broad O–H absorption is consistent with a carboxylic acid group [1].
A 3H singlet is consistent with CH₃ next to a carbonyl carbon with no adjacent hydrogen [1].
CH₃COOH (ethanoic acid) satisfies the molecular formula and gives a separate acidic O–H proton [1].

text: A reaction warms 150.0 g of solution from 20.0 °C to 27.0 °C. A total of 0.0500 mol of limiting reactant reacts. Use c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and ignore calorimeter heat capacity and heat loss. Calculate the molar reaction enthalpy.
scheme: Heat released by the reaction is −4.389 kJ [1].
ΔH = −4.389/0.0500 = −87.8 kJ mol⁻¹ (approximately −88 kJ mol⁻¹ to two significant figures) [1].

text: Given A → B has ΔH = +45 kJ mol⁻¹ and B → C has ΔH = −120 kJ mol⁻¹, determine ΔH for C → A. Explain the principle used.
scheme: For A → C, add the two steps: +45 − 120 = −75 kJ mol⁻¹ [1].
Reverse the process: C → A has ΔH = +75 kJ mol⁻¹ [1].
Hess’s law: enthalpy change depends only on initial and final states, not the pathway [1].

text: For CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), calculate ΔH° using ΔHf°(CH₄) = −74.8, ΔHf°(CO₂) = −393.5 and ΔHf°(H₂O(l)) = −285.8 kJ mol⁻¹.
scheme: Use ΔH° = ΣνΔHf°(products) − ΣνΔHf°(reactants) [1].
ΔHf° for O₂(g), the standard-state element, is zero [1].

text: Write balanced equations for complete combustion of methane and incomplete combustion forming carbon monoxide. Explain why limited oxygen poses an additional health risk.
scheme: Complete combustion: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O [1].
Incomplete combustion to CO: 2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO + 4H₂O [1].
Carbon monoxide is toxic; incomplete combustion can therefore create a serious additional health hazard [1].

text: A reaction has ΔH° = −50.0 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS° = −120 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔG° at 298 K and determine the temperature range for thermodynamic spontaneity under standard conditions, assuming ΔH° and ΔS° are constant.
scheme: Convert ΔS° to −0.120 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ [1].
ΔG° < 0 for T < 417 K; spontaneity does not imply a rapid reaction [1].

text: Calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g). Using molar masses CaCO₃ = 100.09 and CaO = 56.08 g mol⁻¹, calculate the theoretical mass of CaO from 10.00 g CaCO₃ and the percentage yield if 4.80 g CaO is recovered.
scheme: The 1:1 ratio gives 0.09991 mol CaO [1].
Theoretical mass = 0.09991 × 56.08 ≈ 5.603 g [1].

text: A tangent to a gas-volume/time curve passes through (10 s, 20 cm³) and (30 s, 50 cm³). Estimate the instantaneous rate represented by this tangent and explain why it is not necessarily the average rate for the whole reaction.
scheme: Calculate tangent gradient ΔV/Δt = (50 − 20)/(30 − 10) [1].
Rate = 1.5 cm³ s⁻¹ [1].
A tangent estimates the rate at one chosen time; a whole-reaction average uses the overall change and elapsed time [1].

text: At constant temperature, doubling [A] with [B] fixed multiplies the rate by four; doubling [B] with [A] fixed has no effect. When [A] = 0.200 mol dm⁻³, the rate is 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Deduce the rate equation and calculate k with units.
scheme: The reaction is second order in A because doubling [A] gives a fourfold rate [1].
It is zero order in B, so rate = k[A]² [1].
Units of k are dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ [1].

text: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), the forward reaction is exothermic. Predict the effects of increasing pressure, increasing temperature and adding a catalyst on the equilibrium amount of NH₃. State which change alters K.
scheme: Increasing pressure at constant temperature favours the side with fewer gas particles, so increases the equilibrium amount of NH₃ [1].
Increasing temperature favours the endothermic reverse direction, so decreases NH₃ [1].
A catalyst changes neither equilibrium composition nor K; it accelerates attainment of equilibrium [1].
Only temperature changes K here; increasing T decreases K for the exothermic forward reaction [1].

text: 25.00 cm³ of hydrochloric acid is neutralized by 20.00 cm³ of 0.1500 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. Calculate the HCl concentration.
scheme: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O gives a 1:1 mole ratio [1].

text: A buffer contains 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid and 0.150 mol dm⁻³ ethanoate ions. Given Kₐ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, estimate its pH and explain what happens to added small amounts of H⁺.
scheme: Kₐ = [H⁺][CH₃COO⁻]/[CH₃COOH] [1].
Ethanoate removes added H⁺: CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH, limiting the pH change [1].

text: A spontaneous voltaic cell has E°cell = +1.10 V and transfers 2 mol of electrons per mole of reaction. Calculate ΔG° using F = 96,500 C mol⁻¹ and explain the sign.
scheme: Use ΔG° = −nFE°cell [1].
ΔG° = −212 kJ mol⁻¹ to three significant figures [1].
A negative standard Gibbs energy change is consistent with thermodynamic spontaneity under standard conditions [1].

text: Write the initiation step and two propagation steps in the UV-initiated chlorination of methane, then give one termination step.
scheme: Initiation: Cl₂ → 2Cl• under UV light [1].
Propagation: Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + CH₃• [1].
Propagation: CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl• [1].
A valid termination such as Cl• + CH₃• → CH₃Cl or 2Cl• → Cl₂ or 2CH₃• → C₂H₆ [1].

text: Predict the major product when propene reacts with HBr and explain the carbocation argument. Assume ordinary electrophilic addition conditions.
scheme: The major product is 2-bromopropane, CH₃CHBrCH₃ [1].
The π bond initially reacts with H⁺, and protonation can give two possible carbocations [1].
A secondary carbocation, CH₃CH⁺CH₃, is more stable than the alternative primary carbocation [1].
Br⁻ attacks the secondary carbocation, producing the major product [1].
